The letters in the ROAMEF cycle stand for Rationale, Objectives, Appraisal, Monitoring, Evaluation, and Feedback.
A proposal typically progresses through six stages: rationale, objectives, appraisal, monitoring, evaluation, and feedback.
The return on public sector cost (RPSC) measures how effectively an option optimises social value relative to its cost to the public sector.
The RPSC differs from the benefit-cost ratio (BCR) in that it specifically focuses on the public sector's perspective and costs, whereas the BCR considers society as a whole.
The RPSC is described as helpful for comparing different options based on how effectively they optimise social value relative to their cost to the public sector.
The RPSC provides a more nuanced view than the BCR which only captures monetisable social benefits and costs.
The benefit-cost ratio (BCR) is described as the social return of a proposal that captures the monetisable social benefits generated for each pound sterling of monetisable social costs.
Value for money is defined as the balanced judgement about the optimal use of public resources to achieve the objectives of a proposal.
It involves considering the performance of a proposal against its objectives and critical success factors.
It considers costs and benefits that are monetisable and unmonetisable.
It includes distributional effects among different social groups and places.
It considers risk and uncertainty inherent in the proposal.
Value for money optimises social value within a constrained budget.
Social value includes economic prosperity, justice, security, the climate, the environment, people's health and wellbeing.
The Green Book recommends against the use of multi-criteria analysis (MCA) in decision making.
MCA involves simple 'weighting and scoring' that lacks an objective basis and can reduce transparency.
MCDA is used to inform complex technical trade-offs at the longlist stage.
MCDA makes use of swing weighting to objectively weigh the balance of informed expert and stakeholder opinion.
Green rating means the option choice in its category best meets the critical success factors.
Amber rating indicates an option choice that meets the critical success factors but not as well as the green-rated option choice.
Red rating signifies an option choice that does not meet the critical success factors.
Option choices rated red are discarded from the process.
The Green Book uses a value of 1.3 for the elasticity of marginal utility of income.
This value enters the welfare weight as part of the formula: Welfare weight of group = median equivalised income of group / (median equivalised income of national population) × 1.3.
Place-based analysis must assess displacement as an effect beyond additionality and deadweight.
Place-based analysis should consider substitution effects which refer to how interventions might have different impacts in different geographical areas.
Place-based analysis should take into account leakage, considering the quantifiable or qualitative costs and effects of options on different places.
The duty to have due regard to the environmental principles policy statement (EPPS) must be explicitly reflected in appraisals at both the longlist and shortlist stages.
The duty to consider mitigating negative impacts on the environment must be explicitly reflected in appraisals at both the longlist and shortlist stages.
Devolved governments' own statutory duties, where relevant, must be explicitly reflected in appraisals at both the longlist and shortlist stages.

The core principle underlying experimental and quasi-experimental impact evaluation methods is that there is a 'counterfactual'.
The counterfactual involves observed outcomes from a 'control' group that did not receive the intervention.
This counterfactual acts as a proxy for what would have happened to the affected group in the absence of the intervention.

The Four Es in the value for money framework are economy, efficiency, effectiveness, and equity.

Part I – Risk Management Principles Sections (A-E) provide the 'what' and 'why' for an effective risk management framework.
Sections in Part I include Section B: Integration, Section C: Collaboration and Best Information, Section D: Risk Management Processes, Section E: Continual Improvement.

The Orange Book adopts a 'Comply or Explain' approach.

Organizations are required either to disclose compliance with the principles of the Orange Book or to explain their reasons for departure clearly and carefully in their governance statement accompanying their annual resource accounts.
The Orange Book has two parts.
Part I of the Orange Book is titled Management of Risk – Principles and Concepts.
Part II of the Orange Book is titled The Risk Control Framework.
Part I builds on the original Orange Book to improve risk management practices in government organisations.
Part I provides principles for risk management.
Part II offers a structure to categorise existing high-level control requirements.

The fourth pillar of the Risk Control Framework is Standards, Policies & Procedures Approvals

A principal risk is defined as a risk or combination of risks that can seriously affect the performance or reputation of the organisation.
The nature and extent of the principal risks an organisation is willing to take in achieving its objectives should be determined and used to inform decision-making.
The Orange Book characterises risk appetite as the nature and extent of the principal risks that the organisation is willing to take to achieve its objectives.
Organisations should determine and continuously assess their risk appetite.
The Audit and Risk Assurance Committee understands the organisation's policies, attitude to, and appetite for risk.
The board or equivalent senior governance body owns the risk appetite.
Risk management processes must include risk identification and assessment to determine and prioritise how risks should be managed.
Risk management processes must include the selection, design and implementation of risk treatment options that support achievement of intended outcomes and manage risks to an acceptable level.
Risk management processes must include the design and operation of integrated, insightful and informative risk monitoring.

Risk management processes must include timely, accurate and useful risk reporting to enhance the quality of decision-making and to support management and oversight bodies in meeting their responsibilities.

Knowledge Assets are intangible assets that an organisation holds which include inventions, designs, data and information, creative outputs such as text, video, graphics, software and source code, know-how and expertise, business processes, services and other intellectual resources.
Knowledge Assets are valuable public assets which support the effective delivery of public services.
Knowledge Assets can have considerable value and impact beyond their original purpose including social, economic, financial or in combination.
The Rose Book provides guidance on identifying, protecting and exploiting knowledge assets.

A knowledge asset is a piece of knowledge viewed as an asset to the person or organisation which possesses it, including examples such as inventions, designs, data and information, software and source code, expertise and other intellectual resources.

Knowledge Assets under The Rose Book include intangible assets such as inventions, designs, data and information, creative outputs, know-how and expertise, business processes, services, and other intellectual resources.

Another category is Innovation.

A Knowledge Asset Management Strategy should contain three key elements: Strategic Context, Putting KA Management into Practice, and Continuous Evaluation.
Strategic Context sets out the organisational context and management objectives, including who will be accountable for implementing the KAMS and its responsibilities.

Putting KA Management into Practice includes how KA management, decision making and governance will be implemented in the organisation, including how the principles of Identify, Exploit and Protect will be resourced and embedded.
Continuous Evaluation involves evaluating the organisation’s approach to KA management and impact achieved.

The Teal Book is a guidance document that provides a clear, practical model for supporting delivery teams in government.
Its purpose is to enable practitioners and teams to direct and manage portfolios, programmes, and projects successfully and on time.
It supports the Government Functional Standard for Project Delivery.
It offers an overview of project delivery in government.
It describes practices and techniques involved in directing and managing a portfolio, programme, or project.
The Teal Book is structured into 6 parts.
It can be used in varying ways depending on the role or need of the user.
It provides guidance on tailoring which involves adapting its content to suit specific situations within an organization or for particular projects.
Tailoring is essential for effective project delivery and should conform to government functional standards while taking into account internal and external constraints.
The Teal Book can be used as a reference.
Its guidance can be applied in different ways depending on the user's role or needs.
It does not need to be read in full to make use of it.
The Teal Book is underpinned by 3 principles.
Delivery objectives are aligned to government policy and organisational objectives.
Outcomes and enabling outputs meet the identified need and are validated by stakeholders.

The sponsoring body acts as the higher-level authority for a programme or project, providing oversight and acting as the driving force for the work.
It is accountable to a defined higher-level authority, usually the accounting officer of a government department, and through them to ministers and Parliament.
In some cases, the sponsoring body can be an individual, a group, or a board, depending on the programme's or project's context.

The make-up of a sponsoring body can include the portfolio board, its director, the senior official overseeing the policy area, or at organisational level, the executive or departmental management board.
The accounting officer is accountable to Parliament for ensuring that the organisation's actions meet the accounting officer standards of regularity, propriety, value for money and feasibility.
The accounting officer in an arm's length body is usually accountable to the principal accounting officer in the sponsoring department for use of allocated funding as well as to Parliament.
